title: Reading, writing and interpreting texts in digital environments: Editorial introduction
extended_summary:
This paper is an editorial introduction to a special issue on reading, writing, and interpreting texts in digital environments. It frames the broader problem of how digital media, multimodal texts, large language models, and other AI-based tools are changing literacy practices, writing instruction, assessment, and text interpretation in education. The introduction discusses opportunities such as individualized feedback and language support, alongside risks including over-reliance, cognitive offloading, epistemic trust, data protection, and assessment validity.

Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the paper synthesizes and introduces five articles included in the special issue. These contributions cover AI-supported argumentative writing instruction in secondary school, genre-based online support for English email writing in grades 8 and 9, digital environments for judging student texts, AI reliability in literary text interpretation, and virtual reality applications in foreign language teacher education. The editorial emphasizes that digital and AI tools should not be treated as neutral add-ons, but as technologies that reshape how texts are produced, evaluated, and used for learning.

The paper does not provide original participant-level methods, intervention implementation details, or outcome data for a standalone study. Instead, it offers a conceptual overview of the educational challenges and research questions motivating the issue, especially in first, second, and foreign language education. Populations discussed across the issue include secondary students, teachers, and prospective teachers, but the editorial itself does not constitute a direct comparative study of ChatGPT-generated formative feedback on student drafts.

The main conclusion is that productive use of digital and AI-based environments depends on careful pedagogical design, scaffolding, teacher and learner literacies, and critical awareness of limitations and ethical issues. For the user's retrieval topic, this editorial is not direct evidence: it mentions relevant studies, including one cited secondary-school AI-feedback paper, but does not itself report a randomized or quasi-experimental comparison of ChatGPT feedback versus teacher, peer, or no-added-feedback conditions in grades 9-12.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial introduction summarizing a special issue rather than a standalone empirical study. It does not report a clear study design, sample, assignment method, comparator, or analyzable outcome data for a direct secondary-school comparison of ChatGPT feedback versus teacher/peer/no-feedback conditions.
impact_tier_rationale: Direct impact cannot be determined from this editorial because it provides no extractable intervention effects, effect sizes, or outcome statistics from an eligible study. It mentions potentially relevant studies, but this paper itself does not furnish direct evidence of impact.
